## Setup

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("here")
source(here("R", "99_proj_func.R"))
```

## Load data

We load the augmented dataset from the previous step. We use
`mutation_category` to group mutations by where they are in the complex.
We remove the second copy of complex 1DVF, which 02_clean includes twice.

```{r}
dat_aug <- read_csv(
  here("data", "03_dat_aug.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    mutation_category = col_factor(
      levels = c("ab_heavy", "ab_light", "antigen")
    )
  )
) |>
  # 1DVF is an antibody-antibody complex that 02_clean includes twice
  # (roles swapped), so each measurement appears two times. Keep only
  # the copy where the mutated chain is named H or L.
  filter(!(pdb == "1DVF" & !mut_chain %in% c("H", "L")))
```

## Dataset overview

We first count the number of experimental ΔΔG measurements, unique
variants, and complexes. We count measurements and variants separately
because the same variant can be measured more than once. All rows are
single-point mutations, because 02_clean removed multiple mutations,
insertions and deletions. We also count how many measurements have values
for both assay pH and PDB pH.

```{r}
dat_aug |>
  summarise(
    n_measurements = n(),
    n_variants = n_distinct(pdb, mut_chain, mut_position, mut_from, mut_to),
    n_complexes = n_distinct(pdb),
    n_both_ph = sum(!is.na(assay_ph) & !is.na(pdb_ph) & pdb_ph != "na")
  )
```

For single-point measurements, we show the number and percentage on
the antibody heavy chain, antibody light chain, and antigen. If some
measurements have no chain category, we include them as `Unknown` and
keep them in the total used to calculate the percentages.

```{r}
dat_aug |>
  mutate(mutation_category = fct_na_value_to_level(mutation_category,
                                                   level = "Unknown")) |>
  count(mutation_category) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

## Mutations to alanine vs. other amino acids

We compare single-point mutations to alanine with mutations to any other
amino acid. The first panel shows the experimental ΔΔG, followed by one
panel for each computational method. We use the same set of variants
across panels where possible and show the number of measurements in each
group so we can see when the available data differ between panels.

We add a small boxplot inside each violin and a dashed line at ΔΔG = 0.
All groups have more than 200 measurements, so we do not need to show
individual points.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
# Keep only variants that have a prediction from every method,
# so all panels show the same set of variants
ddg_long <- dat_aug |>
  drop_na(ends_with("_ddg")) |>
  select(pdb, mut_chain, mut_position, mut_from, mut_to, to_alanine,
         experimental = ddg, ends_with("_ddg")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(experimental, ends_with("_ddg")),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "ddg"
  ) |>
  drop_na(ddg) |>
  mutate(
    method = str_remove(method, "_ddg"),
    method = fct_relevel(method, "experimental")
  ) |>
  add_target_label()

ddg_long |>
  plot_ddg_violin(
    facet_var = "method",
    y_label = "ΔΔG (kcal/mol)",
    title = "ΔΔG for mutations to alanine vs. other amino acids",
    free_y = TRUE
  )
```

## Experimental ΔΔG by chain

We repeat the alanine comparison using experimental ΔΔG only, with
separate panels for the heavy chain, light chain, and antigen. Each
panel shows the distributions for mutations to alanine and mutations
to other amino acids. We use the same ΔΔG scale across panels so we can
compare the distributions between chains.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
dat_aug |>
  add_target_label() |>
  plot_ddg_violin(
    facet_var = "mutation_category",
    y_label = "Experimental ΔΔG (kcal/mol)",
    title = "Experimental ΔΔG by chain"
  )
```

## Alanine mutation counts by assay pH

For single-point mutations to alanine, we count the measurements at
low and high assay pH for each starting amino acid. For example,
W to A is counted under W. We state the pH cutoff alongside the table
and report how many measurements are missing assay pH. This lets us
see which starting amino acids have enough measurements in both pH
groups for a later comparison.

Some assay pH values are written as ranges or pairs (e.g. `7.3_7.5` or
`6.2 & 7.0`). We use the first number in each value. We use pH 7.4
(physiological pH) as the cutoff: pH 7.4 or lower is low and above 7.4
is high.

```{r}
ala_ph <- dat_aug |>
  filter(to_alanine) |>
  mutate(
    assay_ph_num = parse_number(assay_ph),
    ph_group = case_when(
      assay_ph_num <= 7.4 ~ "low",
      assay_ph_num > 7.4 ~ "high"
    )
  )

# How many alanine measurements are missing assay pH
ala_ph |>
  summarise(missing_assay_ph = sum(is.na(ph_group)))

# Counts per starting amino acid and pH group
ala_ph |>
  drop_na(ph_group) |>
  count(mut_from, ph_group) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ph_group, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(mut_from)
```
